- When sentiment is positive (≥0.2) and forecast is rising steadily, model tends to overestimate and overshoot — reduce later peaks by 5–10%.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.0) and forecast is flat or declining, model often underestimates — raise early lows by 3–7%.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overcorrects and forecasts a prolonged decline — adjust downward slope to match mean reversion.
- In low-sentiment periods, model often fails to capture mean reversion — force a slight upward bias in mid-range to avoid underestimating recovery.
- For 30-day forecasts, if history shows volatility >15% over 5 days, model tends to smooth too much — introduce 1–2% upward adjustment to reflect volatility.
- When sentiment history includes multiple 0.2+ values, model often overestimates — apply a 3–5% downward correction to the final 5–7 days.
- If forecast is flat or slightly rising but true outcome shows sharp drop, model misses downward momentum — add 1–2% downward bias in early days of forecast.
- In high-sentiment periods with recent price spikes, model often fails to account for volatility decay — reduce forecast slope after day 10–15.
